s2.title: What our website offers:
items: Concepts about objects discarded in space
Lessons about the essential components of other prototypes

s3.line1: Places where the site's bots are

home.destLead: Each world tests hardware in a different way: the 14-day lunar night, Martian dust storms, the endless distance of deep space.
home.destMoon: Landing stages, rovers, science stations and memorials from the Apollo era.
home.destMars: Landers, rovers and the first helicopter to fly on another planet.
home.destDeep: Probes that touched an asteroid or are leaving the Solar System.
home.featuredLead: A few pieces that changed space exploration.
home.simLead: Choose a real mission, pick solar panels or a nuclear generator, batteries, insulation, wheels and a computer, and watch your design face the cold, the dust and the radiation day by day.
home.learnTitle: Reuse in space, in the classroom
home.learnLead: Historical precedents, a three-phase teaching method and the robotics behind planetary rovers.

exhibits.title: Collection
exhibits.lead: Every artifact NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and beyond, with what it did and how it could be reused.
exhibits.search: Search by name, mission or place

detail.mapHint: Real surface images from NASA Trek. Drag to move and use + and − to zoom.

missions.title: Missions
missions.lead: From Surveyor 3 in 1967 to Perseverance still at work today: the missions behind every artifact in the collection.

sim.title: Build a probe
sim.lead: Pick a real mission and choose the hardware. The simulator runs day by day through power, temperature, dust, radiation and wear. Values are simplified for teaching.

learn.title: Learn
learn.lead: How to teach robotics through the reuse of space hardware: what already happened, what could happen and how to run it in class.
learn.methodologyLead: Three phases to turn space recycling into a robotics project.
learn.casesLead: Real probes and the parts students can plan to recover.
learn.roboticsLead: Why planetary rovers need autonomy, and how their control is organized.

cascade.perceptionText: The rover uses cameras and sensors to "see" the ground around it: rocks, holes and slopes.
cascade.decisionText: With that picture, it chooses where to go and plans a safe path, avoiding obstacles on its own.
cascade.trajectoryText: It turns the plan into exact moves: how fast to drive and how much to turn at each moment.
cascade.actuatorsText: The wheel motors follow those orders and keep checking themselves, fixing any small error.

learn.calcLead: How much would it cost to send these parts from Earth instead of reusing what is already there?
learn.calcHint: Example value only. Change it to compare scenarios.

nasaMedia.title: NASA images
nasaMedia.text: NASA photos and illustrations are generally not copyrighted and can be used for education, following the NASA media usage guidelines. Each image on the site shows its credit and link.

trek.title: Moon and Mars maps
trek.text: The maps use the surface mosaics of NASA Moon Trek and Mars Trek (Solar System Treks, NASA).

nssdca.title: Mission data
nssdca.text: Names, dates, coordinates and technical details come from the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) and other official NASA pages, linked on each page.

teamImages.title: Team illustrations
teamImages.text: Some images were created by the Spacy Legacy team. They are marked as "Illustration made by our team" and link to the NASA reference used.
